Assistant: I'm glad you're enjoying the weather! As a digital AI assistant, I don't have personal experiences, but I can certainly chat with you about sports and activities. What about you? Do you have a favorite sport or activity that you enjoy during this time of year?
User: Yeah, I'm a huge soccer fan. I love watching professional games and playing with friends on the weekends. There's something about the energy and teamwork that really appeals to me.
Assistant: That's great! Soccer is an amazing sport for building camaraderie and staying active. Have you ever thought about coaching or mentoring young players? You seem really passionate about the sport.
User: Actually, I have thought about it. I've even considered volunteering to coach a local youth team. I think it would be really rewarding to help kids develop their skills and learn valuable life lessons through sports.
Assistant: That's wonderful! Volunteering to coach can be a fantastic way to give back to your community and make a positive impact on young lives. What do you think motivates you to want to coach or mentor young players?
User: I think it's because I had some amazing coaches and role models when I was younger, and they made a huge difference in my life. I'd love to pay it forward and be that positive influence for someone else.
Assistant: It's great that you had positive role models in your life, and now you want to be one for others. Did you know that coaching underprivileged kids can be especially rewarding? They often face unique challenges, and having a supportive coach can make a huge difference in their lives.
User: Yeah, I've actually been thinking about that a lot lately. As a teacher, I've seen firsthand how some kids struggle with access to resources and opportunities. It breaks my heart to think about it.
Assistant: I can understand why it would be tough to see that as a teacher. But it's great that you're thinking about ways to make a difference. Coaching soccer could be an amazing way to connect with those kids and provide them with a positive outlet.
User: You know, it's funny you mention that. My professional life as a teacher is rewarding, but it's my volunteer work coaching underprivileged kids in soccer that gives me a sense of purpose. There's something about seeing them smile and have fun on the field that makes everything worth it.
Assistant: Ah, I can see why that would be so fulfilling for you! It's great that you've found a way to combine your passion for soccer with your desire to make a positive impact on your community. What do you think is the most challenging part of coaching underprivileged kids, and how do you overcome those challenges?
User: One of the biggest challenges is definitely access to resources. Some of the kids don't have the right equipment or transportation to get to practices and games. But I've been lucky to have some amazing community partners who have helped us out with donations and support.
Assistant: That's terrific! It's great that you've been able to find ways to overcome those challenges and provide your team with the resources they need. What advice would you give to someone who is thinking about volunteering to coach underprivileged kids?
User: I would say just go for it! It can be intimidating at first, but the rewards are so worth it. Be patient, be flexible, and be willing to listen and learn from your players. And most importantly, remember to have fun and enjoy the journey!
Assistant: That's fantastic advice! I'm sure you're making a huge difference in the lives of those kids, and it's clear that you're passionate about what you do. Thanks for sharing your story with me today!
User: Doctor, I've been working really hard at soccer practice lately. I want to be the best player on my team.
Assistant: That's great to hear, Patient! Soccer is a great sport to stay active and healthy. How is your training going?
User: It's going well. I've been running laps, doing drills, and practicing my kicks with my teammates every day.
Assistant: That's fantastic! Consistency is key when it comes to improving your skills. Have you noticed any improvements in your performance?
User: Yes, I feel like I'm getting faster and my kicks are getting stronger. But sometimes, I get frustrated because I still make mistakes.

User: That's good advice, Doctor. I'll try to remember that.
Assistant: And if you need any help or advice with your soccer training, don't hesitate to ask. I'm always here to support you.
User: Thank you, Doctor. You're always so kind and supportive, even outside of our appointments.
Assistant: Of course, Patient. I care about your well-being and success, both on and off the soccer field.

User: How do soccer clubs manage and train their goalkeepers?
Assistant: Soccer clubs manage and train their goalkeepers in a number of ways, including:

1. Goalkeeper-specific training: Most professional clubs have goalkeeper coaches who specialize in training and developing the club's keepers. These coaches focus on teaching technique, improving reaction time, and fine-tuning the keepers' game instincts.

2. Fitness training: Goalkeepers need to be fit and agile. They need to work on their strength, coordination, and reflexes to be able to jump, dive, and block shots effectively.

3. Video analysis: Watching videos of one's own matches or those of other goalkeepers can be instructive in analyzing mistakes and finding ways to improve.

4. Tactical and technical training: Goalkeepers need to be knowledgeable about positioning and decision-making under different game scenarios. Coaches teach them how to execute a wide range of skills like distribution, handling, and diving.

5. Communication Training: The keeper's role is essential in directing the defense, and training includes voice commands and body language to guide their team.

6. Simulation training: Training often involves simulating game-like situations to sharpen the goalkeeper's reaction time and decision-making skills.

7. In-game analysis: During matches, the goalkeeper coach will often observe the performance of the keeper and provide useful suggestions or feedback, which can help improve performance.
User: Can goalkeepers improve their agility by practicing other sports?
Assistant: Yes, practicing other sports can help goalkeepers improve their agility. Some sports that can be beneficial for developing agility include basketball, volleyball, and tennis, as they require quick changes in direction and explosive movements.

Basketball can develop quick feet and good reflexes, as it involves jumping, running, and changing direction frequently. Volleyball requires a lot of jumping, which can help improve the agility of goalkeepers for making quick dives to save shots. Tennis demands quick footwork and fast reactions, which can help improve the goalkeeper's ability to react quickly and move rapidly to make saves.

Apart from these sports, other activities like plyometric exercises, yoga, and circuit training can also significantly improve the agility of goalkeepers. Plyometric exercises like jumping squats and box jumps can help develop explosive strength while yoga and circuit training can help in improving overall flexibility and endurance.
User: Have any soccer clubs experimented with using virtual reality to train their goalkeepers?
Assistant: Yes, some soccer clubs have experimented with using virtual reality (VR) to train their goalkeepers. For example, the English Premier League club Manchester City has used VR technology to train its goalkeepers in improving their decision-making skills and improve their reaction time.

Using VR technology enables the goalkeepers to experience simulated game-like scenarios, where they must make split-second decisions in response to real-world situations. The simulations can include different shot types, distances, and angles, allowing goalkeepers to practice their techniques and improve their reactions in a risk-free environment.

VR training allows goalkeepers to make mistakes and learn from them without fear of injury. Coaches can observe the goalkeeper's actions in real-time to provide immediate feedback on technique, positioning, and decision-making. Additionally, VR training can be personalized to the individual needs of each goalkeeper, allowing them to focus on specific areas of their game where they need improvement.

Overall, VR training can be a useful addition to the training regime of soccer clubs and provides an innovative approach to goalkeeper development.
User: It's interesting to see the use of VR technology in training goalkeepers. Do you think other sports could benefit from using VR technology as well?
Assistant: Yes, I think VR technology could be beneficial for other sports as well. Many sports require fast decision-making skills and the ability to react quickly to unpredictable situations. VR technology can help create simulated environments that allow athletes to practice and improve their skills in a safe and controlled environment.

For example, in American football, VR technology can be used to simulate game-like scenarios for quarterbacks to practice their decision-making skills and improve their reaction time in a risk-free environment. In basketball, VR technology can be used to simulate game scenarios for players to practice their shot selection and decision making.

In sports like skateboarding, snowboarding, and surfing, VR technology can be used to create simulations that mimic the experience of being on a board, allowing athletes to practice and improve their technique and decision-making skills.

Overall, I believe VR technology has the potential to revolutionize the way that athletes train and prepare for competition in all kinds of sports. It can provide valuable insights into the athletes' performance and decision-making process, enabling coaches to provide more targeted and effective feedback for improvement.
User: I wonder if VR technology can also be used to train chess players. It could help them practice playing against different strategies and opponents to improve their decision-making skills.
Assistant: Yes, VR technology can be used to train chess players too. Chess players can benefit from VR technology as it can create a three-dimensional and interactive environment for training. It can allow players to play against simulated opponents with varying playing styles, learning their weaknesses and strengths.

VR technology can also be used to create training scenarios for specific challenges faced by the player, making training sessions more targeted towards individual needs. By enabling players to practice in artificial and controlled environments, VR technology can help chess players to make better and more strategic decisions during real matches.

Additionally, chess players can also use VR technology to conduct virtual matches and tournaments, allowing players from different parts of the world to play against each other, without the need to travel to a physical location.

Overall, VR technology can be a useful tool in training and enhancing decision-making skills of chess players. It can create an engaging and immersive training experience that replicates real-world situations and help chess players to prepare better for competition.

c89-m1.summary: The user is an older individual who is retired.
c89-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, how are you doing today?
Assistant: I'm doing well, thank you for asking. How about you? How's your day going so far?
User: It's going alright, I guess. Just a bit stressed about some things on my mind. Nothing too out of the ordinary, though.
Assistant: I'm here to listen if you'd like to talk about what's stressing you out. Sometimes sharing your concerns can help you feel better.
User: Yeah, that's true. I'm just not sure where to start. I've been thinking a lot about my child's future lately.
Assistant: That's completely understandable. As a parent, it's natural to worry about your child's well-being and future prospects. What specifically has been on your mind regarding their future?
User: Well, I just want to make sure they have access to the best possible education. I believe that's key to their success in life.
Assistant: Education is indeed a vital aspect of a child's development. What do you think is the most important factor in ensuring your child receives a good education?
User: Hmm, that's a tough one. I think it's a combination of factors, but having sufficient resources and funding is definitely crucial.
Assistant: That makes sense. Schools and educational institutions often rely on funding to provide quality education and facilities. Have you heard anything recently that's made you concerned about the resources available to your child's school?
User: Actually, yes. There have been rumors of budget cuts in our school district, and I'm worried about how that will impact my child's education.
Assistant: Budget cuts can be challenging for schools, and it's natural to worry about the potential impact on your child's education. What specific concerns do you have regarding the budget cuts?
User: I'm worried that they'll have to cut back on essential programs, like arts and music, or even lay off some of the teachers. That would be really detrimental to the quality of education.
Assistant: Those are valid concerns. Arts and music programs, as well as a sufficient teacher-to-student ratio, are important aspects of a well-rounded education. Have you considered speaking with the school administration or attending a school board meeting to express your concerns?
User: Yeah, I've thought about it. I just don't know if my voice will make a difference.
Assistant: Every voice counts, and as a parent, you have a unique perspective on the issue. By speaking up, you can help raise awareness and advocate for the best interests of your child and their peers. Would you like some help finding resources or information on how to get involved in the decision-making process?
User: Hi, how are you doing today?

Assistant: Hosting international students can be a big responsibility, but also very rewarding. What are some of the challenges you're facing, and how can I assist you?
User: Well, I want to make sure I'm providing the best possible support and guidance for them. They're away from their families and homes, and I want to make sure they feel comfortable and happy here.
Assistant: That's very thoughtful of you. Providing support and guidance to international students can be a bit tricky, especially when it comes to cultural differences and language barriers. Have you encountered any specific issues or concerns that you're not sure how to address?

Assistant: Homesickness is a common issue for international students. One thing you could try is to have an open and honest conversation with them about how they're feeling. User: That's a great idea. I'll definitely try that. What about helping them adjust to the new environment? Do you have any suggestions for that?

User: Those are all great ideas. Thank you so much for your help and advice. I feel more confident now in my ability to support and guide our international students.

User: Write a conversation between a parent and child discussing the importance of education
Assistant: Parent: Hey kiddo, do you know why education is important?

Child: Not really. I just go to school because I have to.

Parent: Well, education is the key to a successful future. It opens up opportunities and helps you achieve your goals.

Parent: You can pursue the career you want, earn a good salary, and have the ability to provide for yourself and your family.

Child: Isn't school just about getting good grades?

Parent: That's part of it, but it's more about acquiring knowledge, skills, and experiences that will help you succeed in your future endeavors.

Child: Okay, but what about people who didn't go to school or didn't finish?

Parent: No problem, kiddo. Education is key, and I want you to have the best future possible.

3. Improved Quality of Life - A good education can lead to better health, higher self-esteem, and a more fulfilling life both personally and professionally.

4. Increased Critical Thinking Skills - Education helps develop critical thinking skills, which are necessary for problem-solving, decision-making, and evaluating information.

5. Growth of Interpersonal Skills - Education helps develop communication, teamwork, and leadership skills, which are essential for success in any field.

User: Here is a piece of text: The Oregon Education Association released a report Tuesday detailing issues in classrooms that disrupt learning and solutions they pose to fix them.
Name calling and profanity. Spitting, kicking and hitting. Ripping books. Brandishing scissors.
These are some of the behaviors educators say are increasing in Oregon classrooms.
Teachers have voiced concerns to the Oregon Education Association over the past few years about disruptive behaviors that not only affect the student doing those things, but also have lasting effects on their peers and educators.
The association released a report Tuesday detailing what they call "a crisis of disruptive learning."
The report delves into these behaviors, what might be causing them and what actions the teachers' union recommends schools, districts, state lawmakers and governmental agencies take to help.
"Now more than ever, we need funding to make sure students get what they need," said John Larson, high school English teacher and president of the Oregon Education Association.
"We also have to realize today ... We have many students with unmet needs," he said. "Housing insecurity, food insecurity, unmet mental-health needs. They have needs in- and outside of school that many of our members are not equipped to deal to with."
School district administrators and Oregon Department of Education staff had not seen the report Monday and could not comment in time for publication.
"While we have not had the opportunity to review the findings, we are committed to building social and emotional learning in Salem-Keizer Public Schools," said Lillian Govus, director of communications for the district.
"By truly understanding what is driving students' behaviors — not just in Salem-Keizer but across the region — we can develop appropriate responses that minimize disruptions and maintain safe educational spaces for our educators and our children," she said.
The report was released just two weeks into Oregon's 2019 legislative session.
Lawmakers are expected to have a large focus on education, especially since the Joint Committee on Student Success is set to develop a comprehensive budget and policy road map to improve K-12 schools.
Colt Gill, director of the Oregon Department of Education, attended the meeting at South Salem High School in November and said there may be legislative opportunities to make these changes happen.
Larson said the association will make sure every legislator has a copy of this report.
While the association estimates another $4 billion over the current service level is needed per biennium to get pre-K through higher education where they need to be, Larson recognized it has to be a long-term, sustainable investment and it won't happen immediately.
The report includes feedback from from hundreds of educators around Oregon. The association, in partnership with the Oregon Department of Education, hosted 14 forums and heard from hundreds of participants online, officials said.
"Oregon is filled with quality educators, quality support professionals who care about every student," he said. "But the conditions in our school make it nearly impossible for them to do their jobs successful.
"We need to make sure we aren't selling our future short."
According to the report, a disruptive learning environment is defined when student behavior significantly interferes with instruction and/or school staff members' ability to maintain a stable classroom or ensure student safety.
At times, these behaviors can become dangerous to the student exhibiting them, or the classroom as a whole.
The report lists myriad negative behaviors educators see regularly — verbal abuse, person-to-person abuse, weaponizing the classroom and destruction of property.
At listening sessions across the state, educators told the association about the "atmosphere of violence that was palpable," of attacks that came regularly and of trauma students experience in that environment.
And while these behaviors may not all be new, educators have reported an increase in the severity and frequency in recent years.
School districts are not required to keep formal data on incidents like "room clears."
A room clear is when students temporarily leave a classroom to reduce the likelihood of injury or trauma as a result of extreme behavior. This typically happens when one student is exhibiting behavior that puts the rest of the class at risk.
The association surveyed educators and students across Oregon on these issues.
Of the respondents, 32 percent said they were scared for students' safety at school, 25 percent said they were concerned for their own safety and 56 percent said their classroom or their child's classroom had experienced at least one room clear this year.
Anecdotally though, many families, administrators and staff have reported to the association that weekly or daily room clears have become commonplace, according to the report.
And according to the bi-annual poll called the Oregon Teaching, Empowering, Leading and Learning survey, educators feel less safe now than they did in 2014, with the percentage of staff who agreed the environment they work in is safe dropping from 92 percent in 2014 to 82 percent in 2018.
"There is not a reliable, timely or effective system in place to intervene when there are consistent disruptions," one respondent told the association. "It feels like a Band-Aid approach."
These behaviors can affect everyone in the classroom.
The student exhibiting the behaviors often lose instructional time and needed supports, and educators said they can experience social isolation and emotional trauma as a result of how peers treat them in the aftermath of the events.
The students witnessing or being harmed by the behaviors also lose out on instructional time, when Oregon already has one of the shortest school years in the country.
Some of these peers have been physically injured. According to the report, others have a hard time learning even when an event isn't occurring due to the stress or fear that something will.
Educators told the association they feel discouraged "that often the only intervention available is for students to be removed from class and 'babysat' in an office, rather than addressing their unmet needs or receive tools to manage their behavior."
"Quite honestly, this is a community problem," Larson said. "This is something that we really need to solve together.
"Our students are at risk," he said. "We need to make sure they are safe and able to learn."
When asked "Why do disrupted learning environments occur?", one participant wrote, "More problems and less support."
The association said decades of "chronic and systemic disinvestment in Oregon schools" is perhaps the most influential reason for this, pointing to the fact that, over the last two decades, the Legislature has consistently financed schools at about 21 to 38 percent below what its own research suggested districts needed to be successful.
However, the report also lists a number of other contributing factors, including increased class sizes; decreased student support specialists; students with high needs but no resources to support them; a marked decreased in "well-rounded education opportunities" and time for physical activity; a lack of appropriate training for educators and an "unclear implementation of policies regarding restraint and seclusion, k-5 expulsion and suspension" and protocols for disruptions.
Not every district is affected by all of these factors, though.
For example, large class sizes are a significant issue in districts like Salem-Keizer Public Schools, which recently passed a capital-construction bond and is planning to change boundaries to address overcrowding.
However, smaller, rural districts aren't usually battling large classes. Instead, they may be facing increased percentages of students who are living in poverty and experiencing homelessness or food insecurity.
And even within one school and one classroom, every student will have their own background and experiences.
"It's different for every, single child," Larson said, adding that's why the state needs more professional development to help better prepare staff. He said additional adults in the classroom and, in some cases, improved curriculum are also needed.
Larson said the goal is to get the resources so each school can look at its population and ask what students need to get the best education possible.
The Oregon Education Association's report includes recommendations that are meant to address the short- and long-term needs in classrooms statewide.
Three key ideas were prioritized — increasing onsite student supports with a focus on mental health, reducing class size and caseloads, and fully funding targeted professional development and ongoing supports for implementation.
Each recommendation includes steps for schools, districts and the state to take.
For onsite supports, the association recommends more mental health counselors, school psychologists, social workers, school nurses, speech language pathologists, occupational and physical therapists and other mental health and trauma experts.
Concerning class size, the state's most recent class size report by the Oregon Department of Education documented 579 classes with 56 or more students.
Additionally, almost half of classes are 35 to 51 percent larger than research recommends, according to the department's report.
Oregon Gov. Kate Brown has recommended paying for additional staff in order to reduce class sizes, especially in K-3 classes, where students are not only learning academic basics, but social norms and appropriate behaviors as well.
And for professional development, the association recommends ongoing training and support for staff to "fully transfer new knowledge into practice."
"We have inadequate training for new curriculum," one teacher told the association. "Teachers in my school are expected to be doing restorative practices/circles regularly in our classrooms; however, not one hour of training has been given so that teachers do this in a truly inclusive and helpful way."
The association recommends staff getting thorough and consistent training on models of trauma-informed practices, social and emotional learning programs and positive behavior programs, to name a few.
Though the report focuses on those three key recommendations, it also includes a number of other ideas that would reportedly help improve safety in schools.
Family wraparound services, increased physical movement and clarified protocols for physical intervention and restraint of students are just a few.
For more information, go to https://www.oregoned.org/ or contact the Oregon Education Association at 503-684-3300.

"We also have to realize today ... We have many students with unmet needs," he said. "Housing insecurity, food insecurity, unmet mental-health needs. They have needs in- and outside of school that many of our members are not equipped to deal to with."
School district administrators and Oregon Department of Education staff had not seen the report Monday and could not comment in time for publication.
"While we have not had the opportunity to review the findings, we are committed to building social and emotional learning in Salem-Keizer Public Schools," said Lillian Govus, director of communications for the district.
"By truly understanding what is driving students' behaviors — not just in Salem-Keizer but across the region — we can develop appropriate responses that minimize disruptions and maintain safe educational spaces for our educators and our children," she said.
The report was released just two weeks into Oregon's 2019 legislative session.
Lawmakers are expected to have a large focus on education, especially since the Joint Committee on Student Success is set to develop a comprehensive budget and policy road map to improve K-12 schools.
Colt Gill, director of the Oregon Department of Education, attended the meeting at South Salem High School in November and said there may be legislative opportunities to make these changes happen.
Larson said the association will make sure every legislator has a copy of this report.
While the association estimates another $4 billion over the current service level is needed per biennium to get pre-K through higher education where they need to be, Larson recognized it has to be a long-term, sustainable investment and it won't happen immediately.
The report includes feedback from from hundreds of educators around Oregon. The association, in partnership with the Oregon Department of Education, hosted 14 forums and heard from hundreds of participants online, officials said.
"Oregon is filled with quality educators, quality support professionals who care about every student," he said. "But the conditions in our school make it nearly impossible for them to do their jobs successful.
"We need to make sure we aren't selling our future short."
According to the report, a disruptive learning environment is defined when student behavior significantly interferes with instruction and/or school staff members' ability to maintain a stable classroom or ensure student safety.
At times, these behaviors can become dangerous to the student exhibiting them, or the classroom as a whole.
The report lists myriad negative behaviors educators see regularly — verbal abuse, person-to-person abuse, weaponizing the classroom and destruction of property.
At listening sessions across the state, educators told the association about the "atmosphere of violence that was palpable," of attacks that came regularly and of trauma students experience in that environment.
And while these behaviors may not all be new, educators have reported an increase in the severity and frequency in recent years.
School districts are not required to keep formal data on incidents like "room clears."
A room clear is when students temporarily leave a classroom to reduce the likelihood of injury or trauma as a result of extreme behavior. This typically happens when one student is exhibiting behavior that puts the rest of the class at risk.
The association surveyed educators and students across Oregon on these issues.
Of the respondents, 32 percent said they were scared for students' safety at school, 25 percent said they were concerned for their own safety and 56 percent said their classroom or their child's classroom had experienced at least one room clear this year.
Anecdotally though, many families, administrators and staff have reported to the association that weekly or daily room clears have become commonplace, according to the report.
And according to the bi-annual poll called the Oregon Teaching, Empowering, Leading and Learning survey, educators feel less safe now than they did in 2014, with the percentage of staff who agreed the environment they work in is safe dropping from 92 percent in 2014 to 82 percent in 2018.
"There is not a reliable, timely or effective system in place to intervene when there are consistent disruptions," one respondent told the association. "It feels like a Band-Aid approach."
These behaviors can affect everyone in the classroom.
The student exhibiting the behaviors often lose instructional time and needed supports, and educators said they can experience social isolation and emotional trauma as a result of how peers treat them in the aftermath of the events.
The students witnessing or being harmed by the behaviors also lose out on instructional time, when Oregon already has one of the shortest school years in the country.
Some of these peers have been physically injured. According to the report, others have a hard time learning even when an event isn't occurring due to the stress or fear that something will.
Educators told the association they feel discouraged "that often the only intervention available is for students to be removed from class and 'babysat' in an office, rather than addressing their unmet needs or receive tools to manage their behavior."
"Quite honestly, this is a community problem," Larson said. "This is something that we really need to solve together.
"Our students are at risk," he said. "We need to make sure they are safe and able to learn."
When asked "Why do disrupted learning environments occur?", one participant wrote, "More problems and less support."
The association said decades of "chronic and systemic disinvestment in Oregon schools" is perhaps the most influential reason for this, pointing to the fact that, over the last two decades, the Legislature has consistently financed schools at about 21 to 38 percent below what its own research suggested districts needed to be successful.
However, the report also lists a number of other contributing factors, including increased class sizes; decreased student support specialists; students with high needs but no resources to support them; a marked decreased in "well-rounded education opportunities" and time for physical activity; a lack of appropriate training for educators and an "unclear implementation of policies regarding restraint and seclusion, k-5 expulsion and suspension" and protocols for disruptions.
Not every district is affected by all of these factors, though.
For example, large class sizes are a significant issue in districts like Salem-Keizer Public Schools, which recently passed a capital-construction bond and is planning to change boundaries to address overcrowding.
However, smaller, rural districts aren't usually battling large classes. Instead, they may be facing increased percentages of students who are living in poverty and experiencing homelessness or food insecurity.
And even within one school and one classroom, every student will have their own background and experiences.
"It's different for every, single child," Larson said, adding that's why the state needs more professional development to help better prepare staff. He said additional adults in the classroom and, in some cases, improved curriculum are also needed.
Larson said the goal is to get the resources so each school can look at its population and ask what students need to get the best education possible.
The Oregon Education Association's report includes recommendations that are meant to address the short- and long-term needs in classrooms statewide.
Three key ideas were prioritized — increasing onsite student supports with a focus on mental health, reducing class size and caseloads, and fully funding targeted professional development and ongoing supports for implementation.
Each recommendation includes steps for schools, districts and the state to take.
For onsite supports, the association recommends more mental health counselors, school psychologists, social workers, school nurses, speech language pathologists, occupational and physical therapists and other mental health and trauma experts.
Concerning class size, the state's most recent class size report by the Oregon Department of Education documented 579 classes with 56 or more students.
Additionally, almost half of classes are 35 to 51 percent larger than research recommends, according to the department's report.
Oregon Gov. Kate Brown has recommended paying for additional staff in order to reduce class sizes, especially in K-3 classes, where students are not only learning academic basics, but social norms and appropriate behaviors as well.
And for professional development, the association recommends ongoing training and support for staff to "fully transfer new knowledge into practice."
"We have inadequate training for new curriculum," one teacher told the association. "Teachers in my school are expected to be doing restorative practices/circles regularly in our classrooms; however, not one hour of training has been given so that teachers do this in a truly inclusive and helpful way."
The association recommends staff getting thorough and consistent training on models of trauma-informed practices, social and emotional learning programs and positive behavior programs, to name a few.
Though the report focuses on those three key recommendations, it also includes a number of other ideas that would reportedly help improve safety in schools.
Family wraparound services, increased physical movement and clarified protocols for physical intervention and restraint of students are just a few.
For more information, go to https://www.oregoned.org/ or contact the Oregon Education Association at 503-684-3300.

User: Hi, I'm Dustin Merton. I noticed that you liked "Will & Grace - Season One." I've been waiting a long time to get the DVD set and I have so much faith in the show. It's the funniest show on television right now. All four of the major characters have unique and special relationships with each other. I can't wait to see the show without commercials.
Assistant: Fascinatingly complex nourish mystery! Have you watched "Bad Education"? Gael Garcia Bernal is terrific in a complicated role. The film is gorgeously shot with a great score. It keeps you absorbed, even if your heart stays a little cool. It's a film that keeps pulling back layers of reality and forces you to reassess what's good, bad, art, and real.
User: That sounds intriguing! I'm definitely interested. Can you tell me more about "Bad Education"?
Assistant: Certainly! "Bad Education" is a film where a filmmaker is reunited with a boyhood lover who wants to tell a dark story from their Catholic school days. But is the story true? And whose story is it really? The film explores themes of hustling, using each other, and the blurred lines between reality and fiction. It has received critical acclaim and is considered one of Almodovar's masterpieces.
User: I'm sold! I'll definitely check out "Bad Education." The complex storyline and the exploration of reality and fiction are right up my alley.
Assistant: I'm glad you're interested! Is there anything else you'd like me to recommend?
User: Thank you for the recommendation, but I think "Bad Education" will keep me occupied for now. I really appreciate your help.
Assistant: You're welcome! If you ever need more recommendations, feel free to ask. Enjoy watching "Bad Education"!
User: Thank you! I'm sure I will. Have a great day!
Assistant: You too! Take care and enjoy your movie.
User: Hello! I've been paying attention to "Making Gay Okay: How Rationalizing Homosexual Behavior Is Changing Everything" and I really enjoyed it. The book provides a great analysis of the propaganda behind changing societal morals and the impact it has had.
Assistant: That's great to hear! It's always fascinating to delve into the complexities of societal changes. How can I assist you today?
User: I would like a recommendation for my next read.
Assistant: Sure! I recommend "Credentialed to Destroy: How and Why Education Became a Weapon". It provides insights into the development of the current education system and the potential consequences.
User: Oh, I've already read that book and found it quite enlightening.
Assistant: I see. In that case, I suggest you check out "When Pigs Fly!: Training Success with Impossible Dogs". It offers valuable tips and techniques for training dogs with challenging behavior.
User: I appreciate the recommendation, but I've actually read that book before too.
Assistant: I apologize for the repetition. In that case, you might be interested in "Original Intent: The Courts, the Constitution, & Religion". It's a comprehensive study on the subject, highly recommended by other readers.
User: That sounds intriguing! Can you tell me more about it?
Assistant: Certainly! According to the review by other readers, this book provides a thorough and well-documented analysis of the courts, the constitution, and religion. It delves into the importance of understanding the original intent behind these institutions and is highly recommended for high schools and universities.
User: That sounds perfect. I'll go ahead and give it a try.
Assistant: Excellent choice! I hope you find it insightful. If you have any more questions or need further assistance, feel free to ask. Enjoy your reading!
User: Thank you! I appreciate your help. Have a great day!
Assistant: You're welcome! Have a wonderful day too!
